comments.author: @sebastianvidret5780
comments.text:
Every problem you described in the video existed before private equity entered youth sports. The real issue is that U.S. pro leagues don't invest in youth development the way clubs in other countries do.

The Miami Heat, for example, have no youth team. Barcelona can afford to develop young players because the academy is subsidized by stadium revenue and TV deals — but also because Barcelona can later sell those players for transfer fees. That's the full economic loop: invest in a kid, then recoup it (and often profit) when he moves on. U.S. pro leagues have no equivalent. A draft pick on a capped rookie contract gives a team no way to "cash out" on a player it developed since age 8, so there's no real business case for the Heat to run an academy even if they wanted to.

Until pro teams run their own youth programs, the cost structure won't change. Top young athletes need to compete against other top athletes, which often means travel. Someone has to pay for court rentals, marketing, and coaching salaries — and the organizers running these programs are the ones absorbing all the financial and legal risk.

Worth adding: even in countries with that club-academy pipeline, it only covers the small slice of kids tagged as elite prospects. The wider base still pays out of pocket for clubs, gear, and travel — pay-to-play doesn't disappear there, it's just narrower at the top. So this really explains the cost of the elite pathway, not the mass-market rec-to-competitive tier, which is where most of the everyday expense actually comes from.

comments.author: @reganator5000
comments.text: The weird thing being that the problem of college sports preventing youth investment was the result of a deliberate policy - the scholarship focussed, oh-so-popular college sports level was deliberately introduced as part of the recruitment stream to pro teams to ensure that good youth players didn't miss out on college, particularly those from poorer backgrounds. Problem is, it was also done when pro players earned much less over the length of their careers and less people went to college - the point was to ensure that pros could get the guaranteed high earnings of a graduate job back when graduate jobs really did guarantee high earnings and playing in the NFL might well leave you unemployed and poor after a few years of pro-level play. Now having been a pro player in those major leagues is probably a better guarantee of employment than the degree that came with their college level scholarship. Especially given that the best youth players won't want a scholarship to the best colleges, because the best colleges for academia tend to be worse at sports than the second-tier state universities, and the big leagues recruit from the best college level teams, rather than giving you bonus credit because you had to put up with harvard's inability to convert all the worlds money into anything above a second division american football team.
